sources.title: Bennett et al. / Seshat (2025), Cliopatria historical polity geometry
sources.access: Pinned archive checked locally; CC BY 4.0. Source geometry and prepared derivatives retain CC BY 4.0: https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/. Whole source polygons simplified at 0.08 degrees, rounded to five decimals and wound for D3; no modern-border tracing.
sources.locator: Archive SHA-256 e10a4e429fca708788ff9e7572a95fce801fae55852d217cffabc1c59cd4eed4; source row indices and raw year windows appear in each territory limit.

sources.title: Bennett et al. (2025), Cliopatria: a geospatial database of world-wide political entities
sources.access: Article access challenged; official data README, licensed archive and methods metadata checked. Historical-atlas reconstructions have uneven temporal resolution.
sources.locator: Scientific Data 12, 247. Dataset years are signed BCE/CE; BCE is converted to astronomical years by adding one.

sources.title: The Secret History of the Mongols, translated by Igor de Rachewiltz, shorter edition edited by John C. Street (2015)
sources.access: Open-access scholarly translation retrieved from the Monumenta Altaica mirror; original Western CEDAR link redirected. Medieval narrative has retrospective and dynastic perspectives.
sources.locator: Sections on the 1206 assembly, Jin campaigns, western conquest and final Tangut campaign; distinguish reported speeches from transcripts.

sources.title: David Morgan, Čengīz Khan (Encyclopaedia Iranica, 1990; revised 2013)
sources.access: Checked 2026-11-18: public institutional text was retrieved. Original synthesis; no source images reproduced.
sources.locator: Early-source limitations; 1206 assembly; Jin invasion in 1211, Qara Khitai in 1218, western invasion in 1219; Jin conquest completed only in 1234.

sources.title: Royal Armouries, Rise of the Mongols
sources.access: Checked 2026-11-18: public institutional text was retrieved. Original synthesis; no source images reproduced.
sources.locator: Tangut invasion 1209; Jin 1211; Qara Khitai 1218; Central Asian city conquests; distinguish subsequent European campaigns.

sources.title: Fenner et al. (2020), Stable isotope and radiocarbon analyses of livestock from Avraga
sources.access: Checked 2026-11-18: public institutional text was retrieved. Original synthesis; no source images reproduced.
sources.locator: Institutional abstract, Archaeological Research in Asia 22:100181, doi:10.1016/j.ara.2020.100181. Main occupation during/perhaps shortly after Chinggis lifetime; later platform use. Publisher-indexed text reports calibrated samples spanning mid-twelfth to fifteenth centuries.

sources.title: Bemmann et al. (2021), Mapping Karakorum, the capital of the Mongol Empire
sources.access: Checked 2026-11-18: public institutional text was retrieved. Original synthesis; no source images reproduced.
sources.locator: Antiquity research article: camp selection 1220, Ögödei city and palace construction 1235, magnetic survey and settlement beyond walls. Survey area is not a population census.

sources.title: Campbell (2021), Cities and the Mongol Conquest: Urban Change in Central Asia 1200–1400
sources.access: Checked 2026-11-18: institutional or publisher-indexed abstract/metadata retrieved; full publication access was unavailable. Claims are limited to the retrieved material.
sources.locator: Oxford DPhil, doi:10.5287/ora-qqxgykxeb. Excavation/radiocarbon synthesis: Otrar shahristan abandonment before 1150; at Merv depopulation/desertion rather than a uniform destruction horizon; later investment.

sources.title: Yuri Bregel, Bukhara iii: After the Mongol Invasion
sources.access: Checked 2026-11-18: public institutional text was retrieved. Original synthesis; no source images reproduced.
sources.locator: Capture in February 1220, later rebuilding and changing administration; narrative accounts of mass violence are not local census data.

sources.title: C. E. Bosworth, Jalāl-al-Din Ḵvārazmšāh(i) Mengübirni
sources.access: Checked 2026-11-18: public institutional text was retrieved. Original synthesis; no source images reproduced.
sources.locator: Gorganj siege in 1221; Parwan and Indus campaigns; competing seasonal dates for the Indus battle, all within 1221.

sources.title: C. E. Bosworth, Nishapur i: Historical Geography and History
sources.access: Checked 2026-11-18: public institutional text was retrieved. Original synthesis; no source images reproduced.
sources.locator: Khwarazmian rule ended with Mongol conquest in 1221; changing urban cores and earlier earthquake damage complicate archaeological attribution.

sources.title: Bāmīān ii: History and monuments (Encyclopaedia Iranica)
sources.access: Checked 2026-11-18: public institutional text was retrieved. Original synthesis; no source images reproduced.
sources.locator: The 1221 assault and medieval urban remains; narrative devastation should not be converted to precise casualty totals.

sources.title: Invisible East Digital Corpus 93: National Library of Israel Ms.Heb.8333.106
sources.access: Checked 2026-11-18: public institutional text was retrieved. Original synthesis; no source images reproduced.
sources.locator: Peer-reviewed edition by Azad and Firoozbakhsh, The Warehouse of Bamiyan (2025), catalogue 16. Administrative mobilisation order, dated approximately 1214–1221; attributed collection geography is not a recorded findspot.

sources.title: Polybius, Histories III, W. R. Paton translation (1922)
sources.access: Public-domain translation retrieved in full through LacusCurtius. Polybius wrote after the war; troop and elephant numbers are ancient reports, not excavated counts.
sources.locator: III.17 Saguntum; 33–35 preparations; 42–56 Rhône and Alps; 60 Taurini; 65–74 Ticinus/Trebia; 78–85 marshes/Trasimene; 107–117 Cannae.

sources.title: Polybius, Histories XV, W. R. Paton translation (1925)
sources.access: Public-domain translation retrieved through LacusCurtius. Fragmentary literary history; battlefield reconstruction and numerical claims require caution.
sources.locator: XV.1 southern Italy and return to Africa; 5–16 the Zama campaign and elephants; 18–19 peace conditions.

sources.title: Livy, Periochae 21–25, translated by Jona Lendering
sources.access: Checked 2026-11-18: public institutional text was retrieved. Original synthesis; no source images reproduced.
sources.locator: Ancient summaries of Livy: 23.1 Capuan alliance; 25.2 Tarentum captured except citadel. Chronological annotations are editorial; for Saguntum use the full Polybian sequence.

sources.title: Livy, Periochae 26–30, translated by Jona Lendering
sources.access: Checked 2026-11-18: public institutional text was retrieved. Original synthesis; no source images reproduced.
sources.locator: 26.1 march near Rome; 26.4 Capua; 26.7 New Carthage; 27.6 Tarentum; 27.13 Hasdrubal at Metaurus; later African campaign. Reported Roman citizen registrations are not Rome city population.

sources.title: Bainbridge and Cracolici (2026; online 2025), Tall talks about elephants: Hannibal’s crossing through disciplines
sources.access: Full open-access article retrieved from author university repository; CC BY 4.0, doi:10.1093/hisres/htaf020. No illustrations reproduced.
sources.locator: Historical Research 99:151–178; competing Alpine routes and limits of modern purported identifications.

sources.title: Martínez Sánchez et al. (2026), The elephant in the oppidum
sources.access: Full author-university abstract retrieved; publisher full-text request was blocked. doi:10.1016/j.jasrep.2026.105577. Limits follow the abstract, not press headlines.
sources.locator: Journal of Archaeological Science: Reports 69:105577. Colina de los Quemados, Córdoba: carpal bone; radiocarbon between fourth and third centuries BCE; associated military context probably Second Punic War, not identity of Hannibal’s own animal.

sources.title: Cartagena Puerto de Culturas, Punic Wall archaeological museum
sources.access: Checked 2026-11-18: public institutional text was retrieved. Original synthesis; no source images reproduced.
sources.locator: Site museum dates Hasdrubal’s foundation to 229 BCE and Scipio’s capture to 209 BCE. Surviving Punic wall is direct site evidence; foundation year follows this museum chronology.

evidence.title: Onon basin: the 1206 assembly
evidence.dateBasis: Dated historical episode in the cited narrative/scholarly chronology; the point is an approximate locality, not a dated archaeological footprint.
evidence.summary: Temüjin’s elevation as Chinggis Khan formalised a newly consolidated steppe coalition.
evidence.limits: Regional anchor in the Onon basin; the assembly’s exact location is not established here. A foundation of political authority is not a newly founded city.

evidence.title: Avraga: archaeology of a proposed imperial camp
evidence.dateLabel: Calibrated samples: mid-12th to 15th centuries; main occupation around Chinggis Khan’s lifetime
evidence.dateBasis: Rounded envelope reported in indexed publication text; individual calibrated ranges and later platform use must not be treated as one continuous settlement interval.
evidence.summary: Livestock radiocarbon supports main occupation during and shortly after Chinggis Khan’s lifetime; some platform use is later.
evidence.limits: Broad envelope of the published calibrated samples, not uninterrupted occupation. The association with a particular ruler is a historical interpretation. No supported resident count is available.

evidence.title: Tangut country: the 1209 invasion
evidence.dateBasis: Dated historical episode in the cited narrative/scholarly chronology; the point is an approximate locality, not a dated archaeological footprint.
evidence.summary: The Mongols invaded Western Xia, whose Tangut rulers controlled northwestern Chinese corridors.
evidence.limits: Yinchuan is a regional-capital anchor, not a surveyed 1209 siege perimeter. This phase did not end the Tangut state.

evidence.title: Northern Jin frontier: invasion in 1211
evidence.dateBasis: Dated historical episode in the cited narrative/scholarly chronology; the point is an approximate locality, not a dated archaeological footprint.
evidence.summary: The campaign against the Jin opened a prolonged war in northern China.
evidence.limits: Zhangjiakou-area marker locates the broad frontier approach, not an authenticated battlefield. Final Jin conquest occurred in 1234, after Chinggis Khan’s death.

evidence.title: Qara Khitai: the western advance
evidence.dateBasis: Dated historical episode in the cited narrative/scholarly chronology; the point is an approximate locality, not a dated archaeological footprint.
evidence.summary: The overthrow of the Qara Khitai realm brought Mongol forces toward Khwarazm.
evidence.limits: The Balasagun-area anchor stands for the regional political transition; it does not claim that Chinggis personally captured this town on a known day.

evidence.title: Otrar: siege and the archaeological problem
evidence.dateBasis: Dated historical episode in the cited narrative/scholarly chronology; the point is an approximate locality, not a dated archaeological footprint.
evidence.summary: Otrar’s siege belongs to the opening western invasion. Excavated abandonment in part of the city predates that assault.
evidence.limits: A burned or deserted urban layer cannot automatically be attributed to 1219. The shahristan abandonment discussed by Campbell had begun by about 1150.

evidence.title: Bukhara: capture and subsequent rebuilding
evidence.dateBasis: Dated historical episode in the cited narrative/scholarly chronology; the point is an approximate locality, not a dated archaeological footprint.
evidence.summary: Bukhara and its citadel fell in 1220; the sources also describe rebuilding under Mongol governors.
evidence.limits: Capture, expulsion and rebuilding are separate processes. Later descriptions of prosperity do not yield a defensible 1220 resident total.

evidence.title: Samarkand: the 1220 conquest
evidence.dateBasis: Dated historical episode in the cited narrative/scholarly chronology; the point is an approximate locality, not a dated archaeological footprint.
evidence.summary: Samarkand fell during the Transoxanian campaign.
evidence.limits: The locality identifies the city region, not the exact extent of destruction. Narrative casualties are not converted into population figures.

evidence.title: Gurganj: the Khwarazmian capital
evidence.dateBasis: Dated historical episode in the cited narrative/scholarly chronology; the point is an approximate locality, not a dated archaeological footprint.
evidence.summary: Mongol commanders besieged and captured the capital in 1221.
evidence.limits: Kunya-Urgench is the historic locality; modern Urgench farther away is not substituted. Destruction traditions require source criticism, not a numerical death toll.

evidence.title: Merv: conquest and changing urban life
evidence.dateBasis: Dated historical episode in the cited narrative/scholarly chronology; the point is an approximate locality, not a dated archaeological footprint.
evidence.summary: Merv experienced a severe contraction around the conquest, while archaeology complicates the familiar picture of a single total-burning event.
evidence.limits: Campbell’s synthesis distinguishes depopulation and desertion from uniform destruction. A precise pre-conquest population and reliable casualty total remain unavailable.

evidence.title: Nishapur: a destructive campaign in 1221
evidence.dateBasis: Dated historical episode in the cited narrative/scholarly chronology; the point is an approximate locality, not a dated archaeological footprint.
evidence.summary: Mongol conquest ended Khwarazmian rule at Nishapur.
evidence.limits: Earlier earthquakes and shifts of the urban core complicate attribution of individual ruins. The marker does not validate the immense death totals in later narratives.

evidence.title: Bamiyan: an administrative voice before conquest
evidence.dateBasis: Date range assigned by the peer-reviewed document edition; modern publication and corpus update dates are excluded.
evidence.summary: A Persian administrative order mobilises commanders and peasants, preserving a local institutional perspective before the conquest.
evidence.limits: The corpus dates the document approximately 1214–1221. The collection’s attributed Bamiyan geography is not a recorded archaeological findspot or proof that its order concerns the Mongol assault.

evidence.title: Bamiyan: the 1221 assault
evidence.dateBasis: Dated historical episode in the cited narrative/scholarly chronology; the point is an approximate locality, not a dated archaeological footprint.
evidence.summary: Accounts connect the city’s devastation with the Mongol attack of 1221.
evidence.limits: Shahr-i Ghulghula and the valley provide a regional anchor. The literary story about vengeance is not a measured casualty series.

evidence.title: Indus: defeat of Jalal al-Din
evidence.dateBasis: Dated historical episode in the cited narrative/scholarly chronology; the point is an approximate locality, not a dated archaeological footprint.
evidence.summary: Chinggis Khan’s army defeated Jalal al-Din near the Indus; the defeated ruler escaped across the river.
evidence.limits: The river-region marker is schematic. Sources differ on the battle’s season, and this map does not assert a proven crossing point or precise day.

evidence.title: Karakorum: the 1220 camp choice
evidence.dateBasis: Dated historical episode in the cited narrative/scholarly chronology; the point is an approximate locality, not a dated archaeological footprint.
evidence.summary: The Orkhon locality selected for an imperial camp became the site of Karakorum under the next khan.
evidence.limits: A camp choice is not the completion of a city. Later walls, streets and palace features must not all be dated to Chinggis Khan.

evidence.title: Western Xia: the final Tangut campaign
evidence.dateBasis: Dated historical episode in the cited narrative/scholarly chronology; the point is an approximate locality, not a dated archaeological footprint.
evidence.summary: The last campaign destroyed the Tangut state; Chinggis Khan died in 1227.
evidence.limits: The capital-region point does not locate his death or burial. Later empire boundaries do not establish his personal conquests.

evidence.title: Karakorum: Ögödei’s city, successor context
evidence.dateBasis: Historical building chronology discussed in the archaeological survey; not the date of the modern survey.
evidence.summary: City and palace construction under Ögödei makes the distinction between the earlier camp and a built imperial capital visible.
evidence.limits: Explicit successor context, not a conquest or urban foundation completed by Chinggis Khan. Surveyed settlement extent cannot be converted directly into a census.

evidence.title: Qart Hadast: the Punic fortified town
evidence.dateBasis: Selected Punic urban phase from the site museum’s historical chronology: foundation assigned to 229 BCE and Roman capture to 209 BCE. Surviving wall remains are archaeological evidence; these are not a single direct radiocarbon interval.
evidence.summary: The surviving Punic wall gives material evidence for the fortified city from which the Barcid campaigns were supplied.
evidence.limits: Foundation in 229 BCE follows the site museum’s chronology; the interval is a selected Punic phase, ending with Scipio’s capture, not the entire life of Cartagena.

evidence.title: Saguntum: siege and the road to war
evidence.dateBasis: Dated historical episode in the cited narrative/scholarly chronology; the point is an approximate locality, not a dated archaeological footprint.
evidence.summary: Hannibal’s siege of Saguntum preceded the invasion of Italy.
evidence.limits: The city anchor does not trace the siege works. Ancient narratives frame responsibility for war from partisan perspectives.

evidence.title: Rhône crossing: people, boats and elephants
evidence.dateBasis: Dated historical episode in the cited narrative/scholarly chronology; the point is an approximate locality, not a dated archaeological footprint.
evidence.summary: Polybius describes a contested river passage and special preparations for transporting elephants.
evidence.limits: The exact crossing site is disputed. This lower-Rhône anchor and the animated line locate a broad episode, not a known ford.

evidence.title: Western Alps: the unresolved pass
evidence.dateBasis: Dated historical episode in the cited narrative/scholarly chronology; the point is an approximate locality, not a dated archaeological footprint.
evidence.summary: The army crossed the Western Alps and entered northern Italy; the identification of the pass remains debated.
evidence.limits: The marker is deliberately regional. Neither the Traversette nor Clapier hypothesis is presented as established, and no elephant-bone identification secures the route.

evidence.title: Taurini: force after the crossing
evidence.dateBasis: Dated historical episode in the cited narrative/scholarly chronology; the point is an approximate locality, not a dated archaeological footprint.
evidence.summary: Polybius reports an attack on the Taurini after the descent into Italy.
evidence.limits: The Turin-area marker approximates an ancient community’s locality; it does not identify an excavated assault horizon.

evidence.title: Ticinus: the cavalry encounter
evidence.dateBasis: Dated historical episode in the cited narrative/scholarly chronology; the point is an approximate locality, not a dated archaeological footprint.
evidence.summary: A cavalry action brought Hannibal into contact with the consul Publius Cornelius Scipio.
evidence.limits: The broader Ticino/Po landscape is shown; the exact battlefield is unresolved and the river system has changed.

evidence.title: Trebia: battle in the river plain
evidence.dateBasis: Dated historical episode in the cited narrative/scholarly chronology; the point is an approximate locality, not a dated archaeological footprint.
evidence.summary: Hannibal defeated a Roman army near the Trebia; elephants belong to the ancient account of this campaign.
evidence.limits: The locality is a river-region reconstruction. Modern field boundaries are not ancient battle lines.

evidence.title: Etrurian marshes: animals and exhaustion
evidence.dateBasis: Dated historical episode in the cited narrative/scholarly chronology; the point is an approximate locality, not a dated archaeological footprint.
evidence.summary: Polybius describes an exhausting marsh crossing and Hannibal riding the surviving elephant.
evidence.limits: The text’s animal count is a reported episode, not a fossil inventory. The wetland corridor is broad and is not a reconstructed 217 BCE shoreline.

evidence.title: Lake Trasimene: the ambush
evidence.dateBasis: Dated historical episode in the cited narrative/scholarly chronology; the point is an approximate locality, not a dated archaeological footprint.
evidence.summary: A Roman army under Flaminius was ambushed beside Lake Trasimene.
evidence.limits: Battlefield proposals differ in detail. The regional point does not authenticate a particular modern memorial or every number in the ancient account.

evidence.title: Cannae: victory without capturing Rome
evidence.dateBasis: Dated historical episode in the cited narrative/scholarly chronology; the point is an approximate locality, not a dated archaeological footprint.
evidence.summary: Cannae was a major Roman defeat, followed by changes in alliances across southern Italy.
evidence.limits: The site anchor is approximate. Ancient force and casualty figures vary and are not used here as population observations.

evidence.title: Capua: alliance and Roman recapture
evidence.dateBasis: Dated historical episode in the cited narrative/scholarly chronology; the point is an approximate locality, not a dated archaeological footprint.
evidence.summary: Capua joined Hannibal’s side after Cannae and was recaptured by Rome in 211 BCE.
evidence.limits: The marker is ancient Capua at modern Santa Maria Capua Vetere, not the later town of Capua. Alliance did not erase local institutions.

evidence.title: Tarentum: city and citadel divided
evidence.dateBasis: Dated historical episode in the cited narrative/scholarly chronology; the point is an approximate locality, not a dated archaeological footprint.
evidence.summary: Hannibal gained Tarentum while the Roman garrison held its citadel; Rome recovered the city in 209 BCE.
evidence.limits: A single city dot cannot express divided control. The surviving Roman citadel is a reason not to colour the whole urban area as uncontested Punic possession.

evidence.title: Near Rome: the 211 BCE diversion
evidence.dateBasis: Dated historical episode in the cited narrative/scholarly chronology; the point is an approximate locality, not a dated archaeological footprint.
evidence.summary: Hannibal moved near Rome while Capua was under siege.
evidence.limits: This was an approach and encampment, not capture of Rome. The Anio-area point is schematic.

evidence.title: Metaurus: Hasdrubal’s failed reinforcement
evidence.dateBasis: Dated historical episode in the cited narrative/scholarly chronology; the point is an approximate locality, not a dated archaeological footprint.
evidence.summary: Hasdrubal’s separate army was defeated before it could join Hannibal.
evidence.limits: This is campaign context, not a battle Hannibal personally commanded. The precise battlefield remains disputed.

evidence.title: Croton and the Lacinian coast: departure for Africa
evidence.dateBasis: Dated historical episode in the cited narrative/scholarly chronology; the point is an approximate locality, not a dated archaeological footprint.
evidence.summary: Hannibal’s remaining Italian base lay in the south before the army returned to Africa.
evidence.limits: The coast anchor does not reconstruct the fleet’s harbour movements or exact sea course.

evidence.title: Zama: the final battle of the war
evidence.dateBasis: Dated historical episode in the cited narrative/scholarly chronology; the point is an approximate locality, not a dated archaeological footprint.
evidence.summary: Scipio and his allies defeated Hannibal’s army; elephants again feature in Polybius’ account.
evidence.limits: Regional Tunisian anchor only: the battlefield identification is disputed. These elephants are not presumed to be the animals that crossed the Alps sixteen years earlier.

evidence.title: Córdoba: a real elephant bone, a limited attribution
evidence.dateLabel: Fourth–third centuries BCE; likely Punic military context
evidence.dateBasis: The author-university abstract reports radiocarbon dating between the fourth and third centuries BCE. The full century envelope is retained; calendar endpoints are display bounds, not exact dated years. The proposed Second Punic War context is a separate archaeological interpretation.
evidence.summary: A carpal bone from Colina de los Quemados was radiocarbon-dated to the fourth–third centuries BCE; associated evidence suggests a Punic military context.
evidence.limits: The 2026 report does not identify an individual animal or tie it to Hannibal’s Alpine column. The broad dating range must remain distinct from the inferred Second Punic War context.

waves.summary: Regional expansion across Central Asia toward the Khwarazmian frontier.
waves.limits: Schematic connection between regional evidence anchors; intermediate vertices improve legibility and are not claimed camps, roads, border crossings or daily progress. No speed, force size or population is encoded. This is an empire-level campaign connection, not a diary of the khan’s personal itinerary.

waves.title: Transoxanian city campaign
waves.summary: The opening invasion and the Bukhara/Samarkand sequence.
waves.limits: Schematic connection between regional evidence anchors; intermediate vertices improve legibility and are not claimed camps, roads, border crossings or daily progress. No speed, force size or population is encoded. Divisions operated separately; a single line does not imply one undivided army.

waves.title: Khorasan: campaigns of Mongol commanders
waves.summary: A connection between the campaign regions of Merv and Nishapur.
waves.limits: Schematic connection between regional evidence anchors; intermediate vertices improve legibility and are not claimed camps, roads, border crossings or daily progress. No speed, force size or population is encoded. This includes commanders such as Tolui, rather than claiming Chinggis personally visited every city.

waves.title: Afghanistan toward the Indus
waves.summary: The southern campaign reached the Indus confrontation with Jalal al-Din.
waves.limits: Schematic connection between regional evidence anchors; intermediate vertices improve legibility and are not claimed camps, roads, border crossings or daily progress. No speed, force size or population is encoded. The final crossing and battlefield are not securely fixed here.

waves.title: Final Tangut campaign
waves.summary: The final war against Western Xia.
waves.limits: Schematic connection between regional evidence anchors; intermediate vertices improve legibility and are not claimed camps, roads, border crossings or daily progress. No speed, force size or population is encoded. The line is not a proposed route to Chinggis Khan’s unknown burial.

waves.title: Iberia to the Rhône
waves.summary: The advance from Iberia into southern Gaul.
waves.limits: Schematic connection between regional evidence anchors; intermediate vertices improve legibility and are not claimed camps, roads, border crossings or daily progress. No speed, force size or population is encoded. The Pyrenean and Rhône crossing points are broad placeholders.

waves.title: Rhône to northern Italy: pass unresolved
waves.summary: A broad western-Alpine crossing followed by northern Italian campaigning.
waves.limits: Schematic connection between regional evidence anchors; intermediate vertices improve legibility and are not claimed camps, roads, border crossings or daily progress. No speed, force size or population is encoded. The central Alpine vertex selects no named pass.

waves.title: From the Po plain into Etruria
waves.summary: The 217 BCE campaign connected the marsh-crossing tradition with Trasimene.
waves.limits: Schematic connection between regional evidence anchors; intermediate vertices improve legibility and are not claimed camps, roads, border crossings or daily progress. No speed, force size or population is encoded.

waves.title: Toward Apulia and Cannae
waves.summary: A broad central-to-southern Italian campaign connection.
waves.limits: Schematic connection between regional evidence anchors; intermediate vertices improve legibility and are not claimed camps, roads, border crossings or daily progress. No speed, force size or population is encoded.

waves.title: Capua and the approach to Rome
waves.summary: A diversion toward Rome during the crisis at Capua.
waves.limits: Schematic connection between regional evidence anchors; intermediate vertices improve legibility and are not claimed camps, roads, border crossings or daily progress. No speed, force size or population is encoded. This route never denotes conquest of Rome.

waves.title: Withdrawal from Italy to Africa
waves.summary: The army’s return to the African theatre.
waves.limits: Schematic connection between regional evidence anchors; intermediate vertices improve legibility and are not claimed camps, roads, border crossings or daily progress. No speed, force size or population is encoded. Maritime vertices are not a reconstructed sailing track.

waves.title: African campaign toward Zama
waves.summary: The campaign culminating in the confrontation with Scipio.
waves.limits: Schematic connection between regional evidence anchors; intermediate vertices improve legibility and are not claimed camps, roads, border crossings or daily progress. No speed, force size or population is encoded. Both approach and battlefield anchor remain regional.

studies.title: Genghis Khan: conquest, camps and cities
studies.summary: Follow the campaigns of 1206–1227, the people and settlements they affected, and the archaeological evidence that complicates the chronicles. A separate 1235 anchor identifies successor-era Karakorum.

studies.title: Hannibal: the campaign and the elephants
studies.summary: Travel from Iberia and the Alps to Italy and Africa, separating ancient testimony, disputed routes and the limited archaeology of war elephants.

territories.title: Carthage: source polity reconstruction
territories.limits: Cliopatria row 679, Carthage, original signed BCE/CE window -230 to -219. Approximate historical-atlas polity reconstruction, not surveyed control or an annual conquest sequence. Source intervals may combine several changes; dated campaign points provide finer event chronology. Whole source geometry retained, simplified at 0.08 degrees and rounded to five decimals; rings oriented for D3. No frontier was inferred from routes or modern borders. CC BY 4.0 source and derivative: Bennett et al. / Seshat, https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/. This represents the Carthaginian polity, not land personally occupied by Hannibal or a uniform administration of allied Italian cities. The last interval may combine battle and subsequent treaty changes.

territories.title: Carthage: source polity reconstruction
territories.limits: Cliopatria row 758, Carthage, original signed BCE/CE window -210 to -209. Approximate historical-atlas polity reconstruction, not surveyed control or an annual conquest sequence. Source intervals may combine several changes; dated campaign points provide finer event chronology. Whole source geometry retained, simplified at 0.08 degrees and rounded to five decimals; rings oriented for D3. No frontier was inferred from routes or modern borders. CC BY 4.0 source and derivative: Bennett et al. / Seshat, https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/. This represents the Carthaginian polity, not land personally occupied by Hannibal or a uniform administration of allied Italian cities. The last interval may combine battle and subsequent treaty changes.
